interactive.title: Walk the loop
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on one circuit. Two batteries, battery 1 on the left and battery 2 on the right, each have their own resistance drawn just above them, and both feed one load, a resistance in the middle branch that they share. That makes two loops: loop 1 runs through battery 1 and the load, loop 2 through battery 2 and the load. Each part carries its example value on the drawing: battery 1 is 12 V with 1 Ω inside, battery 2 is 12 V with 2 Ω inside, and the load is 2 Ω. Each battery's branch has a current arrow, I₁ and I₂, set by a dial underneath that moves in 0.5 A steps from −2 A to 6 A. At the top junction the two currents meet, and the load's arrow shows I₃ = I₁ + I₂, worked out from the dials, because the current flowing into a junction equals the current flowing out. A dial set below zero turns its arrow round and shows its name and size, such as I₂: 1 A, still in ink, because a minus current only means it flows the other way. A tracer, a small ring, sits at the bottom corner of a loop, and you drag it round. Each part it crosses adds its change to a running total beside the loop: plus the battery's voltage when it crosses a battery from − to + (from + to −, minus), and minus I × R when it crosses a resistance in the direction of its current arrow, using V = IR (against the arrow, plus I × R). Back at the start, the total reads 0 V when the dials make that loop's equation true, and otherwise shows what is left over, such as 7 V for loop 1 at the opening 1 A and 1 A. Many pairs bring one loop back to 0, and they lie on one straight line. One screen shows a small grid with I₁ across and I₂ up, 0 to 6 A, with loop 1's line solid and loop 2's dashed, and the dials' pair as a dot; only at the crossing do both totals read 0. Beneath the circuit the working runs line by line: the junction, each loop's walk, the tidied equation, the solve and the check. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. A puzzle shows the circuit with its values and three answers. A wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? shows the walk and the working.
interactive.ignores: The tracer is not the current. It is only a way of adding up voltages, and it can walk against a current's arrow. The voltages and resistances are example figures, with the internal resistances chosen large so each drop is easy to see; they are not a real battery's. Each battery is drawn as a fixed voltage with a fixed resistance inside, but a real battery's voltage and internal resistance change as it charges, discharges and warms up. The wires are drawn with no resistance at all; real cable has a little, which counts as one more resistance in the walk. The dials snap to 0.5 A steps, but the currents can take any value in between. It is DC only: AC circuits use the same two laws with complex numbers, in the Complex numbers course.

explain.text:
A circuit with two loops comes down to two unknown currents, and Kirchhoff's two laws turn it into two equations for them, which you solve as in Elimination. Take two batteries connected side by side to one load, each with a resistance of its own inside it.[^1] That is its [[internal resistance]], and its drop, current × resistance, takes more off the voltage at the battery's terminals as the current rises.[^2] Say, as example values, battery 1 is 12 V with 1 Ω inside, battery 2 is 12 V with 2 Ω inside, and the load is 2 Ω. Battery 1 sends a current I₁, battery 2 a current I₂, and the question is how big each one is. Simpler circuits can be worked out with the series and parallel rules, which is usually easier,[^3] but a circuit like this one, with a battery in two of its branches, cannot be reduced to series and parallel connections,[^4] so it needs Kirchhoff's laws.

The first law is about currents. At a junction, the currents flowing in add up to the currents flowing out.[^5] This is the [[junction law]]. At the top junction I₁ and I₂ flow in and the load's current I₃ flows out, so I₃ = I₁ + I₂. Write I₁ + I₂ wherever the load's current appears, which is Substitution, and only two unknowns are left. The junction at the bottom gives the same equation again, so it adds nothing new.[^6]

The second law is about voltages. Walk once round a loop, adding each rise and each drop of voltage as you pass it, and when you are back where you started the total is zero.[^7] This is the [[loop law]]. One way to picture it: each point in the circuit sits at one voltage level, like a height on a hill, so a walk that ends where it began has dropped exactly as much as it has climbed. Across a resistance the drop is I × R, because the current through it is proportional to the voltage drop across it.[^8] Textbooks add the signs for the walk: crossing a battery from − to + is a rise of its voltage, and crossing a resistance in the direction of its current arrow is a drop of I × R, which counts as a rise when you walk against the arrow.[^9] Walk loop 1, through battery 1 and the load: 12 − 1 × I₁ − 2 × (I₁ + I₂) = 0, which tidies to 3I₁ + 2I₂ = 12. It is the volt drops round a circuit adding up to the supply, written for one loop. A guess shows what the equation does: with I₁ = 1 A and I₂ = 1 A the walk ends at 12 − 1 − 4 = 7 V, not 0, so that pair is wrong. Loop 2, through battery 2 and the load, gives 12 − 2 × I₂ − 2 × (I₁ + I₂) = 0, which tidies to 2I₁ + 4I₂ = 12.

Each law you apply gives one equation, and as many independent equations as unknowns is enough to solve them.[^10] Double loop 1 to get 6I₁ + 4I₂ = 24, and take loop 2 away: 4I₁ = 12, so I₁ = 3 A. Put that into loop 2: 6 + 4I₂ = 12, so I₂ = 1.5 A, and the load carries I₃ = 4.5 A. Walk each loop with these currents and both end at 0: 12 − 3 − 9 = 0 each time. One loop alone is not enough. The pair 4 A and 0 A brings loop 1 back to 0 too, but leaves loop 2 at 4 V. On a grid with I₁ across and I₂ up, each loop's equation is a straight line, and the answer is where the two cross, as in Where two lines meet. Battery 1 gives twice the current because both batteries hold the load at the same 4.5 × 2 = 9 V, so each loses 3 V inside, and 3 V takes 3 A through 1 Ω but only 1.5 A through 2 Ω. You guess each current's direction when you draw its arrow, and a wrong guess just comes out with a minus sign, meaning that current flows the other way.[^11] In this circuit, a minus battery current means the other battery is pushing current backwards through it, as a charger does, which takes a bigger voltage than the battery's own.[^12] This is a teaching model, with each battery a fixed voltage and a fixed resistance inside; a real battery is not quite so steady. **The junction law joins the currents and each loop gives one equation from the loop law, so a two-loop circuit gives two equations in two unknown currents,[^10] which you solve together.**

analogy.text: Picture a round walk in the hills. A chairlift lifts you, as a battery raises the voltage from − to +, and each slope takes you down, as each resistance drops it. Back at the car park, every climb and every descent add up to zero. Two walks that share one slope are like the two loops sharing the load: each walk on its own must still come back to zero.
analogy.breaks: A slope's drop is fixed by the land, however many people walk it, but a resistance's drop is I × R, so it depends on the current through it. That dependence is what turns each walk into an equation in the currents. And nothing flows along a hill path: the walk is only a way of adding up, as the tracer is.

practice.text:
- Draw the circuit. Mark each battery's + and − and every resistance's value, including each battery's internal resistance.
- Draw an arrow for the current in each branch, guessing its direction, and name the unknowns, such as I₁ and I₂.
- At a junction, set the currents in equal to the currents out, and write the third current in terms of the two, such as I₃ = I₁ + I₂.
- Pick two loops, such as one through each battery and the shared load.
- Walk each loop once round. Add a battery's voltage when you cross it from − to +, take it away from + to −. Take away I × R when you cross a resistance along its arrow, add it when you cross against the arrow. Set the total to 0.
- Tidy each loop into the form aI₁ + bI₂ = c.
- Solve the pair by substitution or elimination.
- A minus answer means that current flows against its arrow. Keep the minus in all later working.
- Check: walk each loop again with your answers. Each should end at 0, and the junction should balance.

**Rule of thumb:** one new equation for each unknown. The junction law turns three currents into two unknowns, and two loops give the two equations.

**Worked example:** with example values, a 12 V battery and a 9 V battery, each with 1 Ω inside, feed a 1 Ω load. Loop 1: 12 − 1 × I₁ − 1 × (I₁ + I₂) = 0, so 2I₁ + I₂ = 12. Loop 2: 9 − 1 × I₂ − 1 × (I₁ + I₂) = 0, so I₁ + 2I₂ = 9. Double loop 1: 4I₁ + 2I₂ = 24. Take loop 2 away: 3I₁ = 15, so I₁ = 5 A. Put it back into loop 1: 10 + I₂ = 12, so I₂ = 2 A, and the load carries I₃ = 7 A. Check: loop 1 is 12 − 5 − 7 = 0 and loop 2 is 9 − 2 − 7 = 0. The Second Engineer exam's Marine Electro-Technology syllabus asks for just this: Kirchhoff's-law problems solved by simultaneous equations, two unknowns only.[^13]

**Slips to check for**
- Giving the load only one battery's current. It carries I₁ + I₂.
- Leaving out a battery's internal resistance. Its I × R is a drop like any other.
- Giving a drop the wrong sign when you walk against a current's arrow.
- Using one loop only. A pair that brings loop 1 back to 0 can still fail loop 2.
- Writing the outside loop as a third equation. Walked round the outside, through both batteries, it gives 12 − 1 × I₁ + 2 × I₂ − 12 = 0, so I₁ − 2I₂ = 0, which is loop 1 take away loop 2, so it adds nothing new.
- Taking a minus current for a mistake. It only means the current flows the other way.

checks.label: The sum of all currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it: at every dial setting the load's arrow carries I₁ + I₂, drawn with its size and turned round when it is negative

The algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed loop is zero: with the solved currents both walks end at 0 in all three circuits, and the grid and minus-current screens finish with both totals at 0 V

Each time a rule is applied an equation is produced, and as many independent equations as unknowns can be solved: several dial pairs bring each loop alone back to 0, but exactly one pair fits both, in all three circuits

If a current's direction is assigned wrongly it comes out negative, no harm done: with battery 2 at 4 V, I₂ = −1.5 A, its arrow is drawn turned round with its name and size, I₂: 1.5 A, and both walks still end at 0

Current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage drop across it: each drop is current × resistance, so doubling I₁ from 1 A to 2 A doubles battery 1's inside drop from 1 V to 2 V, and doubling both currents doubles the load's from 4 V to 8 V
The terminal voltage decreases as the current increases, because of the drop across the internal resistance: battery 1's 12 − 1 × I₁ falls at every step up its dial

Every worked line is right, by hand: 7 V and 6 V at 1 A and 1 A; 1 V at 3 A and 1 A; 4 V on loop 2 at 4 A and 0 A; 2 V on loop 1 at 2 A and 2 A; 3 V on loop 2 at 5 A and 0 A with the 10 V and 8 V batteries; the solves give 3 A and 1.5 A, 5 A and −1.5 A, and 4 A and 2 A; and 4 + (−1) = 3 A
Every puzzle has three answers, one of them right, and a hint of its own for each wrong one; the right pair fits both loops and each wrong pair fails at least one

applied.problem: "A circuit with two loops has two unknown currents" is not true as written: it has three branch currents (I₁, I₂, I₃), which the junction law brings down to two, as the lesson itself says two paragraphs later and in the practice.

The walk rule gives only the battery case from − to +; a tracer dragged the other way round crosses a battery from + to −, which subtracts its voltage, so the stated rule is incomplete for half the walks it allows.

The rule of thumb "one equation for each unknown" is more general than the explanation, which needs independent equations; the outside loop is an extra equation that adds nothing, as the slips list says, so it should read one new equation per unknown.

notes.problem: Frozen label mismatch: "Doubled loop 1 take away loop 2: 4I₁ = 12, coefficient of I₁" has value 6, but that coefficient is 4; the 6 is the I₁ coefficient of the doubled loop 1 (6I₁ + 4I₂ = 24). The arithmetic in the text is right.

Frozen label mismatch: "Practice: battery 1's drop 2 × 5, in V" = 10, but battery 1's own drop is 1 Ω × 5 A = 5 V; the 10 is 2I₁ in loop 1 (10 + I₂ = 12), its drop plus the load's share from I₁. The practice text is right.
